![Hero card for Mendral's blog post on frontier-model cost savings. Image from [Mendral](https://www.mendral.com/blog/frontier-model-lower-costs).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Andrea Luzzardi](https://github.com/aluzzardi) at Mendral [reports](https://www.mendral.com/blog/frontier-model-lower-costs) that they now run Opus 4.6 across their CI-triage agent and pay less than they did when everything ran on Sonnet 4.0, because most failures never reach the frontier model at all.

What the article reports:

- **A Haiku "triager" agent fronts the system.** It reads each new CI failure, runs exact-match plus pgvector semantic search against known issues, and decides whether to escalate. Roughly 4 in 5 failures match a known issue and stop there; a triager match costs about 25× less than a full investigation.
- **Opus 4.6 is the orchestrator, not the reader.** It forms hypotheses, then spawns Haiku 4.5 sub-agents with tight prompts ("fetch the exact error from the pnpm install step, return the last 50–100 lines"). Sub-agents are capped at one level deep so fan-out doesn't run away. Haiku absorbs about 65% of input tokens but only ~36% of spend; the input/output ratio is 86:1 for Haiku vs 50:1 for the orchestrator.
- **Logs are pulled, not pushed.** The agent has a SQL interface to ClickHouse and a set of pre-aggregated materialized views; it queries for what it needs rather than receiving 200K-line dumps in the prompt. The authors argue pushing logs front-loads a relevance judgement before you know the cause, and biases the investigation.
- **The pattern only works because both tiers got better.** Six months ago, Sonnet 4.0 wrote bad ClickHouse queries and Haiku 4.0 was useful only for yes/no classification. Opus 4.6 plans well enough to write precise sub-agent prompts; Haiku 4.5 executes narrow scoped tasks reliably. The savings come from the architecture. Both tiers getting good enough made the new shape possible.

## My Notes

- **The headline reads as a model-pricing claim, but the savings are architectural.** "We upgraded and our bill went down" invites the reading that newer models are simply cheaper. They aren't, on a per-token basis. Mendral is running Opus 4.6, priced identically to 4.5; if anything, the trend runs the other way, since [Opus 4.7's new tokenizer raised effective cost ~40% at unchanged sticker pricing](/posts/20260420-opus-47-token-count/). What changed at Mendral is that the expensive model now sees a small fraction of the input. Anyone reading this as "just upgrade" will not see the same bill.
- **The 86:1 input/output ratio is a useful diagnostic for whether your agent has the right shape.** A worker that reads 86 tokens for every 1 it returns is doing what cheap models are good at: absorbing data, returning a focused extract. An orchestrator running closer to 50:1 is synthesizing. If both your tiers come out with similar ratios, you probably haven't actually separated the planning role from the reading role. You're paying frontier prices for token absorption.
- **Capping sub-agents at one level deep is the unglamorous decision that makes the bill predictable.** Recursive agent spawning is the easy default and the easy way to a $40K weekend. The piece notes this in passing, but it's worth pulling out: bounded fan-out is what keeps the cost ceiling in place, and most published multi-agent designs don't impose it.
- **One thing the article doesn't quantify: how much of the win came from the triager vs the better models.** They tell us the triager handles 80% of cases at 25× less cost, and they tell us the upgrade enabled the architecture, but the counterfactual ("Sonnet 4.0 + the same triager pattern") isn't in the post. It would be a useful ablation, especially for teams trying to justify the migration.
